newsitem.title: UK: Suspected IRA rocket hits Belfast court.
newsitem.headline: Suspected IRA rocket hits Belfast court.

text.p: Suspected IRA guerrillas fired a rocket at Belfast High Court on Monday, lightly injuring two people and raising the prospect of retaliation by their pro-British Loyalist foes.
"It looks like some sort of rocket attack," a senior Northern Ireland police officer at the scene said.
Bomb disposal officers combed the area and police sources said the remains of a missile had been found.

Some reports said a masked man stepped calmly from a car in a busy central shopping area, shouldered a rocket launcher and fired a projectile which struck a police security checkpoint outside the court buildings.
A policeman shielded by shatter-proof glass suffered ear injuries and a woman inside the building was blown off her feet by the blast, but there were no serious casualties, police said.
John Hunter, a lawyer in court at the time, said: "I heard a bomb go off, there was momentary shock. We all realised it was a bomb."

There was no immediate claim of responsibility for the attack, which bore all the hallmarks of the Irish Republican Army (IRA), which is fighting to end British rule of Northern Ireland to reunite it with the Irish Republic.
The guerrillas are known to possess rocket-propelled grenades, bazookas and rocket launchers in a vast arsenal assembled on the international black market over two decades.
A car used in the attack was later found abandoned and ablaze in a Catholic section of Belfast -- a guerrilla tactic used to destroy any forensic evidence.
The law courts are a massive complex frequently attacked by the IRA at the height of its anti-British hostilities in the 1970s and 1980s.
It is one of the most heavily guarded points in Belfast and regarded as a key propaganda target by guerrillas because it dispenses British justice and is so tightly protected.

The IRA's ideological enemies, Protestant Loyalists who want Northern Ireland to remain British, said at the weekend they would end a two-year truce and go back to war if the IRA continued its guerrilla campaign.

Loyalists, so-called because of their allegiance to Britain, called a truce in October 1994 to win a seat for their political representatives at multiparty peace talks in Belfast, but say their truce is under severe pressure because of IRA violence.
The IRA bombed British army headquarters in the province last October, killing one soldier and injuring 30, but recent attacks have been botched or foiled by security forces.
On New Year's Eve the guerrillas said they had abandoned a van carying a landmine in the grounds of Belfast castle. Tight security prevented them reaching their target.
The IRA has habitually attacked members of the 12,000-strong Royal Ulster Constabulary and Britain's 18,000 troops in the province during a quarter of a century of guerrilla war.
It ended a 17-month ceasefire last February and is demanding admission of its political arm, Sinn Fein, to the Belfast peace talks without preconditions.
Britain and the Irish Republic, co-sponsors of the talks, say Sinn Fein can only take part when the IRA has called a permanent end to its guerrilla war.
